title: Review: Osmosis and water potential; Active transport, bulk transport and co-transport; The cell cycle and mitosis; Control of the cell cycle and cancer
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CD01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; MB03b#t1 term and clue written for the game; MB04#t2 term and clue written for the game; MB04#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD01a#N.8, CD01b#N.5, CD02a#N.13a, MB03b#N.3, MB04#N.3a, CD01a#N.11, CD01b#N.2, CD02a#N.3, CD01a#N.4, CD02a#N.8, CD01a#N.6a, CD01a#N.10. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anaphase
items.clue: Stage of mitosis in which sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles

items.label: Dilution series
items.clue: Set of sucrose solutions of different strengths made from one stock solution.

items.label: Respiratory inhibitor
items.clue: Substance that cuts a cell's ATP supply, so uptake against a gradient falls sharply.

items.label: Active transport
items.clue: Uptake needing ATP and a membrane protein, able to build a substance up above the outside concentration.

questions.stem: A body cell has 4 chromosomes. It is in anaphase of mitosis. What is moving towards each pole of the cell?

options.text: Two whole chromosomes, each still made of two joined chromatids
Four chromatids: one sister chromatid from each of the 4 chromosomes
One chromosome from each matching (homologous) pair, chromatids still joined
Half of the cell's DNA, which each new cell will replicate after division

questions.explanation: Every chromosome splits at its centromere, and one sister chromatid goes to each pole. Each pole gets a complete, identical set of 4.

questions.stem: In a stained root-tip squash, one cell shows two groups of V-shaped chromatids, their points facing opposite ends of the cell. Which explains this appearance?

options.text: The chromatids are repelling each other and drifting apart; the V shape is the drag of the cytoplasm.
Homologous chromosomes are being separated, each bent at the middle where it was paired.
It is anaphase: spindle fibres attached at each centromere pull it towards a pole, so the arms trail behind.
It is anaphase: the spindle fibres contract like muscle fibres, folding each chromatid in half.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical mammal, protein Q halts the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint when a cell's DNA is damaged and triggers apoptosis if the damage cannot be repaired. A mutation in a skin cell inactivates protein Q. Which statement best explains how this mutation can lead to cancer?

options.text: The cell then divides faster at every stage, and fast division is what makes a cell cancerous.
This single mutation is enough, on its own, to turn the cell into a cancer cell.
The damaged cell divides more often because it needs to replace the cells that died.
Cells with damaged DNA keep dividing, and further mutations build up in their descendants.

questions.stem: A plant cell has a solute potential of −700 kPa and a pressure potential of +200 kPa. What is its water potential?

options.text: −500 kPa
−900 kPa
−700 kPa
+500 kPa

questions.explanation: ψ = ψs + ψp = (−700) + (+200) = −500 kPa. The positive pressure potential raises the water potential above the solute potential.

questions.stem: Root cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water in which the nitrate concentration is much lower than in the cell. When the roots are deprived of oxygen, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What explains these observations?

options.text: Nitrate is taken up by active transport in the same direction as diffusion but faster, and the lack of oxygen slows the diffusion.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP from aerobic respiration, so without oxygen the supply of ATP falls and active transport slows.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP already present in the cell, so removing oxygen must have affected the channel proteins instead.
Nitrate is taken up by facilitated diffusion through channels, which use ATP to move ions across against the gradient.

questions.stem: A population of a hypothetical freshwater plant reproduces only by fragmentation: pieces break off a parent plant and grow into new plants by mitosis. Which claim about the new plants is best supported?

options.text: They carry the same genetic information as the parent, except for any rare new mutations.
They can differ genetically from one another, as each mitotic division mixes up genes.
They may inherit features that the parent developed during its life, such as insect damage.
They each carry only part of the parent's genes, as each fragment receives only some.

questions.stem: Two cells are seen in a stained micrograph of a root tip. Cell 1 has an intact nucleus in which no separate chromosomes can be distinguished. Cell 2 has no nuclear envelope, and its condensed chromosomes lie in a single line across the middle of the cell. Which identification is correct?

options.text: Cell 1 is in prophase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in prophase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in early anaphase.

questions.explanation: An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes is a cell between divisions. Condensed chromosomes aligned at the equator, envelope gone, is metaphase.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of checkpoints in the cell cycle?

options.text: They are points at which a cell moves on automatically once it has grown to a certain size.
They are points at which the cell's progress is held until conditions for the next stage are met.
They are points at which any cell with a problem is destroyed at once, instead of being held there.
They are points in mitosis at which the cell's DNA is replicated, so each daughter cell gets a copy.

questions.explanation: At each checkpoint, conditions such as DNA damage, complete replication or spindle attachment are checked, and the cycle is halted until they are met.

questions.stem: A cell of an organism has 8 chromosomes before its DNA is replicated. How many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules are in its nucleus at metaphase of mitosis?

options.text: 16 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules
8 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules
16 chromosomes, 32 molecules of DNA
8 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules

questions.explanation: Replication gives each of the 8 chromosomes two chromatids, each a DNA molecule: 16 DNA molecules. The chromatids stay joined until anaphase, so there are still 8 chromosomes.

questions.stem: The risk of developing most cancers rises steeply with age. Which explanation fits how tumours form?

options.text: Cells in older people divide faster because the body needs more replacement cells.
A single mutation present from birth suddenly switches on in later life and starts a tumour.
Cancer is simply fast division, and all body cells divide faster as the body ages.
Tumours usually need several mutations in one cell line, which take years to build up.

questions.explanation: Each control gene lost removes one restraint. Collecting several such mutations in one line of cells takes many divisions, and so usually many years.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly gives the sequence of phases in the cell cycle?

options.text: Interphase, made up of G1 and G2, is followed by S, in which the DNA is replicated, and then by mitosis and cytokinesis.
Interphase, made up of G1, S and G2 in that order, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
Interphase, a resting period in which the cell is inactive, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
Mitosis, which occupies most of the cycle, is followed by cytokinesis and then by a short interphase of G1, S and G2.

questions.explanation: G1, S and G2 are the stages of interphase; then mitosis, then cytokinesis. The daughter cells then enter G1 of the next cycle.

questions.stem: A dividing cell is examined after its two new nuclei have formed. Many small vesicles are seen gathering and fusing in a line across the equator of the cell, midway between the nuclei. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: It is a plant cell: the vesicles are assembling sections of new membrane and cell wall to separate the daughter cells.
It is a plant cell: the vesicles mark the line along which the cell membrane will be pinched inwards to split the cytoplasm.
It is a plant cell: the vesicles carry enzymes that soften the existing wall so that it can grow inwards across the cell.
It is an animal cell: the vesicles are new organelles that have been made from scratch so that each daughter cell has a full set.
